sections.title: Concept
sections.content: What Is Microservices Architecture? is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Microservices architecture is an application design approach in which a large application is divided into multiple independently deployable services. Each service owns a clearly defined business capability and communicates with other services through explicit interfaces.

The important idea is not simply "make services small." The real goal is to create boundaries that allow teams to understand, develop, deploy, scale, and evolve parts of a system independently.

A useful mental model is:

```text
Client
   |
   v
```
  API Gateway
```text
     |
+----+-----------------------------+
|          |          |            |
```
  v          v          v            v
Customer   Order      Payment     Notification
Service    Service     Service       Service
```text
|          |           |             |
```
 DB         DB          DB            DB

Each service can contain its own business logic, integration adapters, and persistence mechanism. The service exposes an API or participates in asynchronous messaging.

A microservice should normally represent a meaningful business responsibility rather than an arbitrary technical layer.

Examples of useful boundaries include:

- Customer management
- Product catalog
- Order management
- Payment processing
- Inventory
- Shipping
- Notification
- Trip management
- Driver management

The boundary should be driven by business responsibility, ownership, change patterns, and data ownership.

sections.content:
Worked example for **What Is Microservices Architecture?**:

```text

```

The flow illustrates the relationship described in the explanation. The important part is to understand what crosses the service boundary and which component owns the responsibility.

Now trace one successful request and one failed dependency. Identify the boundary, the owner, and the failure behavior.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content:
- Use **What Is Microservices Architecture?** when deciding how a service should be structured or integrated with the rest of the system.
- Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.
- Use the described communication approach when decoupling, buffering, or event propagation is important.
- Apply the data-ownership guidance when deciding where state should live and how changes should propagate between services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of What Is Microservices Architecture? as a design decision with a boundary and a cost. Start with the business capability and ownership, then trace communication, data, deployment, failure handling, and observability. A pattern is successful when it improves those properties for the actual workload rather than simply increasing the number of services.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content:
Interview focus for **What Is Microservices Architecture?**:
- Define the pattern in terms of the problem it solves, not only its name.
- Explain where the boundary sits and which component owns the responsibility.
- Discuss latency, partial failure, retries, compatibility, observability, and operational cost where relevant.
- Give one concrete example and one case where you would avoid the pattern.
- Be ready to compare it with the closest alternative and explain the trade-off.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content:
Common pitfalls:
- Splitting services by technical layers rather than business capability.
- Choosing a pattern before identifying the actual constraint.
- Ignoring operational ownership and observability.
- Assuming distributed architecture is automatically more scalable or reliable.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
When to use / avoid **What Is Microservices Architecture?**:

Use it when the problem described by the topic is significant enough to justify the additional distributed-system complexity. Prefer a simpler design when the capability is small, changes together with its neighbors, has no meaningful independent scaling or ownership requirement, or would gain little from the extra boundary.

Before adopting it, check four questions: Who owns it? What contract crosses the boundary? What happens when the dependency is slow or unavailable? How will the team observe, deploy, and recover it?

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Production scenario — **What Is Microservices Architecture?**:

Imagine an e-commerce platform with independently operated Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **What Is Microservices Architecture?** to the point where this topic affects the request path or event flow. Define the owning service first, then identify the network interaction, timeout/deadline, failure behavior, observability signals, and recovery path. A production design should specify what happens during partial failure instead of describing only the successful flow.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Monolithic Architecture is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A monolithic application may still be logically modular internally. It can contain modules for customers, orders, billing, notifications, payments, and other capabilities. The important difference is that these modules are packaged and deployed as one application.

For a Java application, the deployment unit might be a JAR or WAR. Other platforms use their own packaging mechanisms.

A monolith has several attractive properties during the early stages of development:

- One deployment unit
- Simple local development
- Straightforward debugging
- Easy end-to-end testing
- Simple communication between modules
- One database can make transactions and queries convenient
- Few operational components are required

A small application can therefore be very successful as a monolith.

The problem appears when the application continuously grows.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:
Worked example — **Monolithic Architecture**:

Consider an e-commerce flow involving Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **Monolithic Architecture** to one concrete interaction in that flow. Identify the caller, the receiving service, the contract, the data or event crossing the boundary, and the expected result. Then ask what should happen if the receiving service is slow, unavailable, or returns a duplicate result. This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

topics.title: Why a Monolith Can Become Difficult
topics.description: As features accumulate, the codebase becomes harder to understand. Developers may need knowledge of many modules before making a seemingly local change.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Why a Monolith Can Become Difficult is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
As features accumulate, the codebase becomes harder to understand. Developers may need knowledge of many modules before making a seemingly local change.

Typical consequences include:

- Longer development cycles
- More difficult debugging
- Larger regression risk
- Longer build and startup times
- More difficult deployments
- Difficulty scaling individual capabilities
- Difficulty adopting new technologies
- Greater coordination between teams

A change to one module can require rebuilding and redeploying the complete application.

Suppose image processing consumes significant CPU while customer management mainly needs memory. With one deployment unit, both capabilities may have to run on the same infrastructure profile. You cannot independently scale the image processing capability without also scaling unrelated functionality.

Reliability can also become coupled. A memory leak in one module can consume resources belonging to the complete application process.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The term "monolithic hell" describes the situation where a once-manageable application becomes so large and interconnected that development and deployment become painful.

Common symptoms are:

- Nobody understands the complete system
- Small changes have unpredictable side effects
- Releases require extensive coordination
- Deployment takes too long
- Testing becomes increasingly expensive
- Teams are blocked by unrelated changes
- Old technology choices become difficult to replace
- Scaling is performed for the whole application instead of individual capabilities

The important lesson is that the problem is not that monoliths are inherently bad. The problem is allowing a growing system to become tightly coupled and difficult to evolve.

topics.title: Microservices as a Complexity Management Strategy
topics.description: Microservices attack complexity by decomposing the application into manageable services. The total business functionality does not disappear.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Microservices as a Complexity Management Strategy is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Microservices attack complexity by decomposing the application into manageable services.

The total business functionality does not disappear. Instead, it is divided into boundaries.

For example:

```text
Large Application
    |
    +-- Customer Management
    +-- Driver Management
    +-- Trip Management
    +-- Billing
    +-- Payments
    +-- Notifications
```
Each capability becomes a separate service.

The result is a distributed system rather than a single process.

This introduces new complexity:

- Network communication
- Service discovery
- Partial failures
- Distributed data
- Deployment coordination
- Monitoring
- API compatibility
- Operational automation

Therefore, microservices trade one kind of complexity for another. They are most useful when the benefits of independent evolution and scaling outweigh the additional distributed-system complexity.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Service Boundaries is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A good service boundary should isolate a coherent business capability.

A useful boundary normally has:

- A clear responsibility
- A clear owner
- Its own business rules
- A well-defined API
- Controlled access to its data
- A manageable rate of change
- A meaningful deployment boundary

Avoid creating services solely because a class or database table exists.

For example, creating separate services for CustomerNameService, CustomerAddressService, and CustomerPhoneService may produce excessive network communication and operational overhead.

A better boundary might be Customer Management if those capabilities normally change and operate together.

For example:

```text
REST / Messaging API
        |

Application / Domain Logic
        |
        v
Persistence Adapter
        |
        v
   Service Database
```

This keeps implementation details behind the service boundary.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Independent Deployment is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
One of the strongest benefits is independent deployment.

If the Order Service changes but the Customer Service does not, the Order Service can be built, tested, and deployed without redeploying the Customer Service.

This enables:

- Smaller releases
- Faster feedback
- Reduced deployment coordination
- Safer incremental changes
- Continuous delivery
- Team autonomy

Independent deployment only works when service contracts are designed for compatibility.

sections.content:
Worked example — **Independent Deployment**:

Consider an e-commerce flow involving Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **Independent Deployment** to one concrete interaction in that flow. Identify the caller, the receiving service, the contract, the data or event crossing the boundary, and the expected result. Then ask what should happen if the receiving service is slow, unavailable, or returns a duplicate result. This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

- Use **Independent Deployment** when deciding how a service should be structured or integrated with the rest of the system.
- Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.
- Use the deployment guidance to choose an appropriate runtime boundary and automate repeatable delivery.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Independent Deployment as a change-management and runtime concern.
```text
Catalog:       3 instances
Order:         8 instances
Payment:       4 instances

```
If Order processing receives a traffic spike, additional Order instances can be started without duplicating unrelated services.

This can also allow different infrastructure profiles for different services.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The Scale Cube describes three dimensions of scaling:

X-axis — horizontal duplication
```text
Run multiple identical copies of a service or application.
```
Y-axis — functional decomposition
```text
Split the application according to business capabilities.
```
Z-axis — data partitioning
```text
Route or partition data based on a meaningful attribute such as customer identity or another key.
```
Microservices primarily correspond to Y-axis scaling.

X-axis scaling example:

```text
Load Balancer
  /   |   \
```
   App1 App2 App3

Y-axis scaling example:

```text
 Gateway
   |
+--+---------+
|    |       |
```
 Order Catalog Payment

Z-axis scaling example:

```text
 Customer ID
    |
+---+---+
|       |
```
Shard A  Shard B

Real systems can combine these approaches.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Database per Service is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A core microservices principle is that each service owns its data.

Instead of:

```text
All Services -> One Shared Database
```
prefer:

```text
Order Service    -> Order Database
Customer Service -> Customer Database
Payment Service  -> Payment Database
```
The data is private to the owning service and should normally be accessed through its API or events.

This creates loose coupling.

If every service directly queries another service's tables, the services become coupled to the database schema and independent deployment becomes much harder.


sections.title: Practical use

- Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.
- Use the described communication approach when decoupling, buffering, or event propagation is important.
- Apply the data-ownership guidance when deciding where state should live and how changes should propagate between services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Database per Service through ownership of state. In microservices, the difficult part is rarely storing data; it is deciding which service is authoritative, how other services obtain information, and how a business operation behaves when updates span multiple data owners. Make consistency requirements explicit before choosing a pattern.

- Sharing database tables across service boundaries.
- Assuming distributed transactions are automatically available or cheap.
- Ignoring stale or eventually consistent reads.
- Making one service depend on another service's internal schema.
- Forgetting idempotency and reconciliation for multi-step workflows.

sections.content:
Different services may use different storage technologies.

Examples:

- Relational database for transactional orders
- Search engine for full-text search
- Graph database for relationship-heavy data
- Document database for flexible documents
- Key-value store for fast lookups

This is called polyglot persistence.

The benefit is that each service can choose storage according to its workload.

The cost is operational complexity: the organization must understand and manage multiple technologies.

topics.title: Benefits of Microservices
topics.description: Major benefits include: Complexity management Large systems are divided into understandable units. Team autonomy Teams can focus on individual services.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Benefits of Microservices is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Introduction To Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Major benefits include:

1. Complexity management
   Large systems are divided into understandable units.

2. Team autonomy
   Teams can focus on individual services.

3. Independent deployment
   Services can be released independently.

4. Independent scaling
   High-demand services can be scaled separately.

5. Technology flexibility
   Different services can use suitable implementation technologies.

6. Better fault isolation
   Failure in one service does not automatically require every service to stop.

7. Easier modernization
   A service can be replaced or rewritten independently.

8. Organizational alignment
   Service ownership can match team ownership.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: API Composition is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Api Gateway area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Suppose a client requests:

```text
GET /product-details?id=100
```
The gateway may internally perform:

```text
Product Service
Review Service
Inventory Service
Recommendation Service
Shipping Service
```

sections.content:
Every remote request should have a finite timeout.

```text
Gateway -> Service
          waits forever
```

```text
Gateway -> Service

          +-- timeout
          |
          +-- fallback / error
```
Timeouts should be chosen according to realistic service latency and user requirements.

sections.title: Concept

The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Inside a monolith, modules can call each other's methods directly.

In microservices, services are separate processes, often running on different machines.

Therefore communication must cross a process or network boundary.

This introduces:

- Network latency
- Serialization
- Connection failures
- Timeouts
- Authentication
- Retries
- Version compatibility

A remote call is fundamentally different from a local method call.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Publish/Subscribe is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
One producer publishes an event and multiple interested consumers receive it.

```text
Order Service
     |
     v
  Channel
  / | \
 v  v  v
```
  Email Audit Analytics

The publisher does not need to know every consumer.

sections.title: Worked example

```text
Order Service
     |
     v

 v  v  v
```

sections.title: Practical use

- Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.
- Use the described communication approach when decoupling, buffering, or event propagation is important.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Publish/Subscribe as a time and ownership boundary. A message allows the sender and receiver to avoid sharing the same execution moment, but it does not remove the need for contracts, delivery semantics, idempotency, ordering decisions, and failure handling. Ask who owns the event, who consumes it, and what happens if delivery is delayed or repeated.

- Ignoring duplicate messages and missing idempotency.

- Assuming ordering is global when it is only guaranteed within a narrower scope.
- Retrying without considering poison messages or retry storms.

topics.description: For messaging, the API includes: Channel names Message types Message fields Delivery expectations Error handling Ordering requirements Consumer behavior

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: API Definition for Messaging is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Inter-Process Communication area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
For messaging, the API includes:

- Channel names
- Message types
- Message fields
- Delivery expectations
- Error handling
- Ordering requirements
- Consumer behavior

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:
Worked example — **API Definition for Messaging**:

Consider an e-commerce flow involving Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **API Definition for Messaging** to one concrete interaction in that flow. Identify the caller, the receiving service, the contract, the data or event crossing the boundary, and the expected result. Then ask what should happen if the receiving service is slow, unavailable, or returns a duplicate result. This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content:
- Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.
- Use the described communication approach when decoupling, buffering, or event propagation is important.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of API Definition for Messaging as a time and ownership boundary. A message allows the sender and receiver to avoid sharing the same execution moment, but it does not remove the need for contracts, delivery semantics, idempotency, ordering decisions, and failure handling. Ask who owns the event, who consumes it, and what happens if delivery is delayed or repeated.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content:
Interview focus for **API Definition for Messaging**:
- Define the pattern in terms of the problem it solves, not only its name.
- Explain where the boundary sits and which component owns the responsibility.
- Discuss latency, partial failure, retries, compatibility, observability, and operational cost where relevant.
- Give one concrete example and one case where you would avoid the pattern.
- Be ready to compare it with the closest alternative and explain the trade-off.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content:
Common pitfalls:
- Assuming delivery is exactly once without verifying the actual system semantics.
- Ignoring duplicate messages and missing idempotency.
- Treating message schemas as private implementation details.
- Assuming ordering is global when it is only guaranteed within a narrower scope.
- Retrying without considering poison messages or retry storms.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
When to use / avoid **API Definition for Messaging**:

Use it when the problem described by the topic is significant enough to justify the additional distributed-system complexity. Prefer a simpler design when the capability is small, changes together with its neighbors, has no meaningful independent scaling or ownership requirement, or would gain little from the extra boundary.

Before adopting it, check four questions: Who owns it? What contract crosses the boundary? What happens when the dependency is slow or unavailable? How will the team observe, deploy, and recover it?

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Production scenario — **API Definition for Messaging**:

Imagine an e-commerce platform with independently operated Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **API Definition for Messaging** to the point where this topic affects the request path or event flow. Define the owning service first, then identify the network interaction, timeout/deadline, failure behavior, observability signals, and recovery path. A production design should specify what happens during partial failure instead of describing only the successful flow.

topics.title: API Evolution
topics.description: Microservice clients cannot always be upgraded simultaneously. During rolling deployment, old and new service versions may coexist.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: API Evolution is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Inter-Process Communication area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Microservice clients cannot always be upgraded simultaneously.

During rolling deployment, old and new service versions may coexist.

Therefore API changes should be backward compatible whenever practical.

A safe additive change might be:

```text
Existing response:
{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Alice"
}

New response:
{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "Alice",
  "preferredLanguage": "en"
}
```
Old clients should ignore unknown fields.

A new service version should provide sensible defaults for missing fields when appropriate.

```text
}
```

The flow illustrates the relationship described in the explanation. The important part is to understand what crosses the service boundary and which component owns the responsibility.

Now trace one successful request and one failed dependency. Identify the boundary, the owner, and the failure behavior.

topics.title: Partial Failure
topics.description: A distributed call can fail because: Service is down Network is unavailable Service is overloaded Service responds slowly DNS or routing fails Connection pool is exhausted…

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Partial Failure is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. In the Inter-Process Communication area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A distributed call can fail because:

- Service is down
- Network is unavailable
- Service is overloaded
- Service responds slowly
- DNS or routing fails
- Connection pool is exhausted
- Dependency itself has failed

The caller must assume that remote operations can fail.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Partial Failure as controlling the blast radius of dependency failure. A remote dependency can be slow, unavailable, or partially broken. Good resilience design prevents one failure from consuming all threads, connections, retries, or queue capacity and defines a deliberate degraded behavior.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content:

- Setting timeouts longer than the caller's useful deadline.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Thrift Serialization and Transport is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Inter-Process Communication area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Thrift can work with different encodings and transports.

Binary encodings are generally more compact and efficient to process than verbose human-readable representations.

HTTP can be useful where network compatibility is important, while direct transports may provide different performance characteristics.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:
Worked example — **Thrift Serialization and Transport**:

Consider an e-commerce flow involving Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **Thrift Serialization and Transport** to one concrete interaction in that flow. Identify the caller, the receiving service, the contract, the data or event crossing the boundary, and the expected result. Then ask what should happen if the receiving service is slow, unavailable, or returns a duplicate result. This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: - Treat the interface as an explicit contract so consumers can evolve without depending on internal implementation details.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Thrift Serialization and Transport as a remote interaction, not a local method call. The network introduces latency, serialization, timeouts, authentication, compatibility issues, and partial failure. The right choice depends on whether the caller needs an immediate answer, eventual processing, fan-out, or durable delivery.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content:
Interview focus for **Thrift Serialization and Transport**:
- Define the pattern in terms of the problem it solves, not only its name.
- Explain where the boundary sits and which component owns the responsibility.

- Give one concrete example and one case where you would avoid the pattern.
- Be ready to compare it with the closest alternative and explain the trade-off.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content:
Common pitfalls:
- Treating a remote call like an in-process call.
- Omitting timeouts and bounded concurrency.
- Ignoring serialization and contract compatibility.
- Making long synchronous chains that amplify latency and failure.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
When to use / avoid **Thrift Serialization and Transport**:

Use it when the problem described by the topic is significant enough to justify the additional distributed-system complexity. Prefer a simpler design when the capability is small, changes together with its neighbors, has no meaningful independent scaling or ownership requirement, or would gain little from the extra boundary.

Before adopting it, check four questions: Who owns it? What contract crosses the boundary? What happens when the dependency is slow or unavailable? How will the team observe, deploy, and recover it?

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A useful architecture separates:

1. Client tier
2. Delivery tier
3. Aggregation/data tier
4. Services tier

The delivery tier can handle routing, load balancing, caching, and security.

The aggregation tier can expose high-performance APIs and coordinate access to backend services.

The services tier contains business capabilities and service-specific data.

This structure helps keep client concerns separate from backend implementation details.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Why Service Discovery Is Necessary is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Service Discovery area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Microservice instances often have dynamic network locations.

Instances can be:

- Started
- Stopped
- Replaced
- Rescheduled
- Scaled
- Moved

Hard-coding:

```text
order-service = 10.4.3.10:8080
```
is fragile in a dynamic environment.

The system needs a way to discover currently available instances.

- Use the deployment guidance to choose an appropriate runtime boundary and automate repeatable delivery.
- Use discovery and health information instead of relying on fixed service-instance locations.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Why Service Discovery Is Necessary as dynamic topology management. Service instances can appear, disappear, move, or scale, so callers need a reliable way to locate healthy destinations. Discovery must be paired with health information, timeouts, and sensible load distribution.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A service registry maintains information about service instances.

A conceptual registry entry may contain:

```text
Service: order-service
Host: 10.4.3.20
Port: 8080
Health: available
Metadata: version, zone, region
```
The registry normally needs:

- Registration API
- Deregistration capability
- Query API
- Health/heartbeat mechanism
- High availability
- Consistency appropriate to the environment

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Why Distributed Data Is Difficult is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Event-Driven Data Management area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
In a monolith, a transaction can update several tables in one database.

**Example**

```text
BEGIN TRANSACTION
  update customer
  insert order
  update inventory
COMMIT
```
The database provides ACID guarantees.

With microservices, each service may own a different database.

Now a business operation may require:

```text
Customer DB
    +
Order DB
    +
Inventory DB
    +
Payment DB
```
A single local database transaction cannot automatically cover all of them.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
ACID represents:

Atomicity:
All changes in a transaction succeed together or are rolled back.

Consistency:
A successful transaction leaves the database in a valid state.

Isolation:
Concurrent transactions do not expose invalid intermediate states as if they were committed results.

Durability:
Committed data survives normal failures according to the database's durability guarantees.

ACID makes multi-row, multi-table changes relatively straightforward inside one database boundary.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Eventual Consistency is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Event-Driven Data Management area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
With event-driven data management, all services may not observe a change at exactly the same moment.

**Example**

```text
Order created
    |
    +--> Inventory receives event
    |
    +--> Payment receives event
```
For a short period, one service may show the old state while another has already updated.

This is eventual consistency.

The system is designed so that, assuming successful processing, related state converges over time.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Idempotent Consumers is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. In the Event-Driven Data Management area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Messages can sometimes be delivered more than once.

Therefore consumers should be designed so repeated processing does not corrupt business state.

For example, if Inventory receives:

```text
InventoryReserved(order=100)
```
twice, the second processing should recognize that reservation 100 has already been applied.

Common techniques include:

- Idempotency keys
- Processed-event tables
- Unique constraints
- State checks

sections.content:

```text

```

The flow illustrates the relationship described in the explanation. The important part is to understand what crosses the service boundary and which component owns the responsibility.

Now trace one successful request and one failed dependency. Identify the boundary, the owner, and the failure behavior.

sections.title: Practical use

sections.title: Deep mental model

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A monolith may have a small number of identical runtime instances.

A microservices application may have:

- Many services
- Multiple instances per service
- Different languages
- Different frameworks
- Different resource requirements
- Different scaling policies
- Different deployment schedules

Automation therefore becomes essential.

sections.title: Practical use

- Apply the incremental approach when moving an existing application toward independently deployable services.

sections.content: Think of Why Deployment Is More Difficult as a change-management and runtime concern. A service boundary is valuable when a team can build, test, release, and operate that capability with limited coordination.   +--> Queue

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Do Not Rewrite Everything at Once is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Refactoring A Monolith Into Microservices area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A large existing application should generally not be rewritten from scratch merely to adopt microservices.

A complete rewrite creates a large period where:

- Existing features still need maintenance
- New features still need delivery
- The replacement system is incomplete
- Teams must understand old and new systems
- Business risk increases

Incremental migration is safer.

This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content:
- Use **Do Not Rewrite Everything at Once** when deciding how a service should be structured or integrated with the rest of the system.
- Apply the incremental approach when moving an existing application toward independently deployable services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Do Not Rewrite Everything at Once as a design decision with a boundary and a cost. Start with the business capability and ownership, then trace communication, data, deployment, failure handling, and observability. A pattern is successful when it improves those properties for the actual workload rather than simply increasing the number of services.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Existing modules can gradually become independent services.

**Example**

```text
Monolith
  |
  +-- Customer
  +-- Order
  +-- Inventory
  +-- Reporting
```
Extract Inventory:

```text
Monolith
  |
  +-- Customer
  +-- Order
  +-- Reporting

Inventory Service
  |
Inventory DB
```
The monolith becomes smaller after every extraction.

topics.title: Idempotency
topics.description: An operation is idempotent if repeating it produces the same intended final state. For distributed systems, idempotency is critical because retries can cause duplicate requests.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Idempotency is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Cross-Cutting Architectural Concepts area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An operation is idempotent if repeating it produces the same intended final state.

For distributed systems, idempotency is critical because retries can cause duplicate requests.

**Example**

```text
PUT /customers/10
same request repeated
```
can safely produce the same customer state.

For payment operations, idempotency keys are especially important so a retry does not accidentally charge twice.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:

sections.content:

```text
   |

   |
Database
```

- Timeouts
- Bulkheads
- Concurrency limits
- Circuit breakers
- Backpressure
- Graceful degradation

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: When to Prefer Synchronous Communication is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Architectural Decision Guide area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Synchronous communication is useful when:

- The caller needs an immediate result
- The operation is short
- Failure should be visible immediately
- The dependency is part of the request's critical path

**Example**

```text
Checkout -> Payment Authorization
```

sections.title: Deep mental model

The network introduces latency, serialization, timeouts, authentication, compatibility issues, and partial failure. sections.title: Concept
sections.content: When Not to Split a Service is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Architectural Decision Guide area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Avoid extraction when:

- The boundary is unclear
- The services would constantly call each other
- Data is inseparable
- Independent deployment provides no meaningful benefit
- The operational cost exceeds the business benefit

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content:
Worked example — **When Not to Split a Service**:

Consider an e-commerce flow involving Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **When Not to Split a Service** to one concrete interaction in that flow. Identify the caller, the receiving service, the contract, the data or event crossing the boundary, and the expected result. Then ask what should happen if the receiving service is slow, unavailable, or returns a duplicate result. This makes the architectural trade-off visible instead of treating the pattern as a diagram-only concept.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content:
- Use **When Not to Split a Service** when deciding how a service should be structured or integrated with the rest of the system.
- Apply the data-ownership guidance when deciding where state should live and how changes should propagate between services.
- Use the deployment guidance to choose an appropriate runtime boundary and automate repeatable delivery.
- Apply the incremental approach when moving an existing application toward independently deployable services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of When Not to Split a Service as a design decision with a boundary and a cost. Start with the business capability and ownership, then trace communication, data, deployment, failure handling, and observability. A pattern is successful when it improves those properties for the actual workload rather than simply increasing the number of services.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content:
Interview focus for **When Not to Split a Service**:
- Define the pattern in terms of the problem it solves, not only its name.
- Explain where the boundary sits and which component owns the responsibility.
- Discuss latency, partial failure, retries, compatibility, observability, and operational cost where relevant.
- Give one concrete example and one case where you would avoid the pattern.
- Be ready to compare it with the closest alternative and explain the trade-off.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content:
Common pitfalls:
- Splitting services by technical layers rather than business capability.
- Choosing a pattern before identifying the actual constraint.
- Ignoring operational ownership and observability.
- Assuming distributed architecture is automatically more scalable or reliable.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
When to use / avoid **When Not to Split a Service**:

Use it when the problem described by the topic is significant enough to justify the additional distributed-system complexity. Prefer a simpler design when the capability is small, changes together with its neighbors, has no meaningful independent scaling or ownership requirement, or would gain little from the extra boundary.

Before adopting it, check four questions: Who owns it? What contract crosses the boundary? What happens when the dependency is slow or unavailable? How will the team observe, deploy, and recover it?

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Production scenario — **When Not to Split a Service**:

Imagine an e-commerce platform with independently operated Catalog, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Notification services. Apply **When Not to Split a Service** to the point where this topic affects the request path or event flow. Define the owning service first, then identify the network interaction, timeout/deadline, failure behavior, observability signals, and recovery path. A production design should specify what happens during partial failure instead of describing only the successful flow.

topics.title: Failure Example
topics.description: Suppose Inventory is unavailable. Order Service may still record the order and publish the event.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Failure Example is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the End-To-End Microservices Example area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Suppose Inventory is unavailable.

Order Service may still record the order and publish the event.

The Inventory Service processes the event later.

This creates eventual consistency.

If the business requires the order to remain pending until inventory is confirmed, the Order Service can represent states such as:

```text
PENDING
   |
inventory reserved
   |
CONFIRMED
```
The state machine makes asynchronous progress explicit.

sections.content:
Worked example for **Failure Example**:

```text

   |
inventory reserved
   |
CONFIRMED
```

The flow illustrates the relationship described in the explanation. The important part is to understand what crosses the service boundary and which component owns the responsibility.

Now trace one successful request and one failed dependency. Identify the boundary, the owner, and the failure behavior.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content:
- Use **Failure Example** when deciding how a service should be structured or integrated with the rest of the system.
- Use the described communication approach when decoupling, buffering, or event propagation is important.
- Apply the data-ownership guidance when deciding where state should live and how changes should propagate between services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Failure Example as controlling the blast radius of dependency failure. A remote dependency can be slow, unavailable, or partially broken. Good resilience design prevents one failure from consuming all threads, connections, retries, or queue capacity and defines a deliberate degraded behavior.

sections.title: Interview focus

- Give one concrete example and one case where you would avoid the pattern.

- Setting timeouts longer than the caller's useful deadline.
- Adding fallbacks that silently return unsafe or misleading data.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A complete microservices architecture can be understood as a set of connected responsibilities:

```text
BUSINESS BOUNDARIES
      |
      v
INDEPENDENT SERVICES
      |
      +------------------+
      |                  |
      v                  v
  SYNCHRONOUS        ASYNCHRONOUS
  COMMUNICATION      COMMUNICATION

      +--------+---------+
               |
               v
         SERVICE DISCOVERY
               |
               v
          DATA OWNERSHIP
               |
               v
      EVENTUAL CONSISTENCY
               |
               v
          DEPLOYMENT
               |
      +--------+---------+
      |        |         |
      v        v         v
     VM     Container  Serverless
               |
               v
          AUTOMATION
               |
               v
          OBSERVABILITY
               |
               v
         RESILIENT SYSTEM
```
The most important architectural principles are:

1. Split by meaningful business capability.
2. Give services clear ownership.
3. Keep data private to the owning service.
4. Communicate through explicit contracts.
5. Expect network calls to fail.
6. Use timeouts and resilience mechanisms.
7. Use asynchronous events where decoupling is valuable.
8. Design APIs for independent evolution.
9. Automate deployment and operations.
10. Scale services according to their individual needs.
11. Do not create tiny services simply for the sake of size.
12. Migrate large existing applications incrementally.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Final Revision Summary is a microservices architecture concept concerned with how services are separated, connected, operated, or evolved. The key question is not whether the pattern sounds modern, but what problem it solves, what boundary it creates, and what new failure or operational cost it introduces. In the Quick Comparison Tables area, reason from business responsibility, service ownership, contracts, data flow, and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Microservices are best understood as an architectural approach for controlling complexity in large, continuously evolving applications.

The architecture begins with meaningful business boundaries. Each service owns a focused capability and normally controls its own data.

Because services run as independent processes, communication must be designed deliberately. Synchronous request/response is useful when an immediate result is required. Asynchronous messaging is useful for decoupling, buffering, event propagation, and one-to-many communication.

An API Gateway can provide a stable client-facing entry point while hiding internal service structure. Service discovery solves the problem of dynamically locating service instances.

Private service-owned databases improve independence but create distributed data-management challenges. Event-driven architecture, local transactions, event records, transaction-log techniques, event sourcing, CQRS, and materialized views provide different ways to manage those challenges.

Deployment must be automated because a real microservices system can contain many services and many runtime instances. Virtual machines, containers, and serverless functions represent different deployment trade-offs.

When starting with an existing monolith, incremental migration is safer than a complete rewrite. New functionality can be built separately, presentation and backend layers can be separated, and existing modules can be extracted one at a time.

The central lesson is:

```text
Microservices are not primarily about making things small.

They are about creating boundaries that allow software
to evolve, deploy, scale, and fail independently.
```
A successful architecture balances:

```text
Business boundaries
+ API design
+ Communication
+ Data ownership
+ Resilience
+ Discovery
+ Deployment
+ Automation
+ Observability
```
When these concerns are designed together, microservices can provide the organizational and technical independence needed by large, evolving applications.

A pattern is successful when it improves those properties for the actual workload rather than simply increasing the number of services.
